sections.heading: The AEC industry map: who designs, who builds, who does both
bullets: The architecture/engineering/construction world splits into design firms (sell drawings, calculations, and stamped professional judgment), contractors (sell built work), and EPC hybrids (sell both under one contract) — the trade press ranks them on separate lists precisely because the businesses differ

The Engineer of Record (EOR) is the licensed professional who stamps the design and carries legal responsibility for it — design firms sell that accountability, which is why 'who designed it' matters as much as 'who built it' on critical infrastructure

Design-bid-build separates the two (owner hires a designer, then bids the construction); design-build merges them into one contract for speed and single-point accountability — the delivery model data-center and power clients increasingly demand

A firm can be a giant on one list and mid-pack on the other: design revenue counts fees (high margin, low dollars), construction revenue counts the whole built cost (huge dollars, thin margin) — so a #7 designer at #35 contractor is a design-led hybrid, not a contradiction

sections.heading: Transmission lines: what actually gets built between substations
bullets: Transmission voltages ladder up (69 → 115 → 230 → 345 → 500+ kV) because higher voltage moves more power with less loss over distance; a project's voltage class tells you its role — 115 kV feeds local areas, 230 kV+ moves bulk regional power

A line project is mostly not wire: right-of-way acquisition (easements across hundreds of parcels), environmental review, structure design (lattice towers vs monopoles), foundations, and stringing — the land and permitting work often outweighs the construction

'Rebuild' projects re-conductor or re-tower an existing corridor to raise capacity — faster than new-build because the right-of-way already exists; that's why utilities serving new data-center load often rebuild old 115 kV lines while adding new 230 kV ones
Undergrounding costs several times overhead and complicates repairs, so it's reserved for cities and crossings; underwater (submarine) cable is its own specialty for islands and offshore wind

sections.heading: Interconnection: the queue that gates the AI buildout
bullets: Nothing connects to the grid without an interconnection study: engineers model what the new generator or load does to power flows, voltages, and fault currents, then price the network upgrades needed to accommodate it — the requester typically funds those upgrades

The studies run in queued phases (feasibility → system impact → facilities) and the queue is the bottleneck: in busy regions the wait runs years, which is why data centers cluster where capacity exists and why bridge power exists at all

Generation interconnection (a solar farm feeding in) and load interconnection (a gigawatt campus drawing out) are different studies with different rules — and regulators have recently begun writing large-load rules specifically because AI campuses broke the old assumptions

For engineering firms this is annuity work: every hyperscale site spawns studies, substation designs, and utility upgrade programs — paid on the regulated utility side regardless of which GC wins the building

sections.heading: Global engineering centers: how a substation gets designed overnight
bullets: Large AEC firms run offshore engineering centers (India is the hub) where hundreds of engineers execute detailed design — drawings, calculations, BIM models — for projects across the globe

The model works because detailed design is separable: a US-licensed EOR sets criteria and reviews/stamps the work, while production engineering follows the sun — a substation package advanced overnight is on the lead engineer's desk by morning

Economics compound with scale: an offshore engineer at a fraction of US cost, multiplied across thousands of drawings per project, materially changes a design firm's margin — and relieves the domestic engineering-talent shortage that AI-era power demand has made acute
The constraint is knowledge transfer and licensure: codes, utility standards, and stamping authority stay onshore, so the offshore center amplifies senior engineers rather than replacing them

sections.heading: OT cybersecurity: protecting the machines, not the email
bullets: IT security protects information systems; OT (operational technology) security protects the control systems that run physical infrastructure — SCADA, relays, PLCs, plant controls — where a breach doesn't leak data, it opens breakers or damages equipment

OT environments invert IT priorities: availability beats confidentiality (you cannot patch-and-reboot a running substation), gear lives for decades, and many protocols predate security entirely — so defense leans on segmentation, monitoring, and engineered fail-safes

US bulk-power systems operate under mandatory NERC CIP standards (critical infrastructure protection) with real fines — one reason utilities buy specialized OT-security consulting rather than generic IT services

'Cyber-informed engineering' pushes security into the design itself: engineering physical systems so that even a successful cyber intrusion cannot command a dangerous state — a discipline engineering firms are natively positioned to sell

sections.heading: Public procurement: rules, points, and protests
bullets: Public owners (cities, utilities' municipal cousins, airports) buy through structured competitions — scored proposals, selection committees, published criteria — because they spend public money; private hyperscalers can simply pick, public owners must justify

Many jurisdictions score MWBE/DBE participation (minority- and women-owned business enterprise commitments): teams pledge partnership percentages to win points, and delivering on those pledges is both contract obligation and political trust — reneging invites lawsuits and debarment risk

Losing bidders can protest, litigate, or arbitrate: procurement disputes over scoring, conflicts of interest, and insider influence are a recurring feature of billion-dollar public competitions, and confidential arbitrations can move tens of millions years after award

For firms whose franchise is utility and municipal work, procurement reputation is the balance sheet: one adverse diversity-compliance finding can outweigh years of technical excellence in the next selection committee's scoring

flashcards.q: What is the Engineer of Record (EOR)?
flashcards.a: The licensed professional engineer who stamps a design and carries legal responsibility for it. Design firms fundamentally sell that stamped accountability — which is why 'who designed it' matters as much as 'who built it' on critical infrastructure.

flashcards.q: Why can a firm rank #7 as a designer but #35 as a contractor without contradiction?
flashcards.a: The two lists count different money: design revenue counts fees (high margin, small dollars), construction revenue counts the entire built cost (huge dollars, thin margin). A design-led EPC hybrid ranks high on fees and mid-pack on construction volume.

flashcards.q: Design-bid-build vs design-build — what's the difference?
flashcards.a: Design-bid-build separates the contracts: the owner hires a designer, then competitively bids construction. Design-build merges both under one contract for speed and single-point accountability — the model power and data-center clients increasingly demand.

flashcards.q: Why does transmission voltage climb in steps like 115, 230, 345, 500 kV?
flashcards.a: Higher voltage moves more power with less loss over distance, but costs more in insulation, clearance, and equipment. Each class has a role: 115 kV feeds local areas, 230 kV+ moves bulk regional power. A project's voltage class tells you its function.

flashcards.q: Why is a transmission-line project mostly not about the wire?
flashcards.a: Right-of-way acquisition (easements across hundreds of parcels), environmental review, structure design, and foundations usually dominate cost and schedule. That's also why 'rebuild' projects in existing corridors move faster than new builds — the land fight is already won.

flashcards.q: What is an interconnection study and who pays for the upgrades it identifies?
flashcards.a: Engineering analysis of what a new generator or large load does to grid power flows, voltages, and fault currents. It prices the network upgrades required — and the requesting party typically funds them. No study, no connection.

flashcards.q: Why do interconnection queues gate the AI buildout?
flashcards.a: Studies run in queued phases (feasibility → system impact → facilities) and busy regions have years-long waits. That delay drives data-center siting toward existing capacity, spawns bridge-power generation, and pushed regulators to write new large-load interconnection rules for gigawatt campuses.

flashcards.q: How can a substation be designed 'overnight'?
flashcards.a: Global capability centers: offshore engineering teams (India is the hub) produce detailed drawings, calculations, and BIM models while the US sleeps, under criteria set — and later stamped — by the onshore Engineer of Record. Follow-the-sun production amplifies scarce senior engineers.

flashcards.q: How does OT security differ from IT security?
flashcards.a: IT protects information; OT protects the control systems running physical infrastructure (SCADA, relays, PLCs). Priorities invert: availability beats confidentiality, equipment lives decades, and legacy protocols predate security — so defense relies on segmentation, monitoring, and engineered fail-safes rather than patch cycles.

The mandatory Critical Infrastructure Protection standards governing cybersecurity of the North American bulk power system, enforced with real fines. Compliance obligations are a key reason utilities buy specialized OT-security consulting instead of generic IT services.

Designing the physical system so that even a successful cyber intrusion cannot command a dangerous state — safety margins, mechanical interlocks, and fail-safes engineered in from the start. It treats cybersecurity as an engineering-design property, not just a software layer.

flashcards.q: What are MWBE commitments in public procurement, and why do they carry teeth?
flashcards.a: Pledged participation percentages for minority- and women-owned business partners, scored in proposal evaluations. They're contract obligations and political trust: reneging invites lawsuits, debarment risk, and reputational damage that outweighs technical excellence in future selection scoring.
